questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: State what warrants extending a finding past one case
questions.stem: A cartographer notes that a headland plotted from one survey flight came out slightly rotated. What would warrant carrying that correction into the whole projection?

options.text: The cartographer's confidence in the instrument, since a trusted instrument settles how far the error spreads.
options.misconception: takes instrument reliability as a warrant for extending a finding

options.text: The number of times the error appeared on the same sheet, since repetition on one sheet reaches the whole projection.
options.misconception: counts repeats on one sheet as if they covered the projection

options.text: That the error came from a distortion affecting the whole survey, and the other sheets share that survey.
That the client asked for the correction, since a request from the client is a reason enough to extend it.
options.misconception: accepts a client's request as a warrant for a general finding

questions.explanation: A correction carried past one observation needs a reason to think the same cause runs through the rest. A survey-wide distortion is such a reason; instrument reliability and a client's request are not.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same cause would reach the other sheets.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: Explain the warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.stem: A cartographer generalises from one surveyed estuary to all estuaries on the sheet. Explain what the generalisation rests on and what would strengthen it.

answer.exemplar: The generalisation rests on a warrant, and the warrant is that the surveyed estuary is typical of the others: that the features which produced its shape are shared rather than peculiar to it. A case-based generalisation always leans on some such assumption, whether or not the cartographer writes it down, and a reader cannot evaluate the claim unless the assumption is stated. The warrant would be strengthened by surveys of estuaries that differ from the first one in size, sediment and tidal range, since a finding that holds across such differences is not resting on the accidental features of the first case.

questions.explanation: A generalisation from one case rests on a warrant, the assumption that the case is typical of the others. It must be stated so a reader can weigh it, and surveys of differing estuaries would strengthen it.
questions.hint: Ask what assumption about the case it needs.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: Say what test a case chosen for its promise performs

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that a projected straight-line course was checked by comparing the chart with the movements of a boat's log. The notes say the course was chosen because the first leg promised a clean line, and a second leg that promised nothing was left out of the check.

questions.stem: Given this note, what test does checking the promised leg perform?

options.text: It tests whether every course on the sheet is drawn correctly, since a checked leg is evidence about the others.
options.misconception: treats one checked leg as evidence about all the other courses

options.text: It tests the cartographer's eyesight, since reading a bearing off a log is a visual task.
options.misconception: turns a case check into a question about the checker's eyesight

options.text: It tests whether the log itself is accurate, since a wrong log would make the check meaningless.
options.misconception: reframes the case as a test of the log rather than of the promise

options.text: It tests the promise the chosen leg was picked for, so the case checks the reason it was chosen.

questions.explanation: A case chosen for a promise is picked to show something, and checking it tests that expectation. One checked leg says nothing about the rest, and the log's accuracy is a separate question.
questions.hint: Ask what the case was chosen to reveal.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a deviant case obliges an explanation to add
questions.learningObjective: State what a deviant case obliges an account to add
questions.stem: A river mapped by two survey teams takes a sharp turn where the teams' data disagree. What does the deviant case oblige the account to add?

options.text: An element that the ordinary case does not require, so that the account can cover the turn as well as the straight reaches.
A replacement for the ordinary case, since an account that fits the deviant case must discard the others.
options.misconception: treats a deviant case as grounds for discarding the rest

options.text: A separate projection, since the deviant reach cannot be shown on the same sheet as the rest.
options.misconception: insists a deviant case needs its own projection to be shown

options.text: Nothing at all, since a deviant case is dropped from an account and reported as an aside.
options.misconception: believes deviant cases are excluded from an account

questions.explanation: A deviant case obliges the account to add what the ordinary case does not need, so it covers the turn and the straight reaches alike. Excluding the case would leave the account untested.
questions.hint: Ask what the ordinary case fails to account for.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for establishing that an ordering was necessary
questions.learningObjective: Plan how to show that an ordering was necessary
questions.stem: A cartographer records that the contour survey preceded the levelling, and the levelling preceded the published sheet. What should the cartographer do to show that the order mattered?

options.text: State that the sequence was efficient, since a smooth order of work shows that each stage was needed.
options.misconception: treats a tidy order of work as evidence that stages were needed

options.text: Show that the later stage would have been wrong or impossible had the earlier one been done in the other order.
Repeat the sequence in the notes, since a repeated record makes the necessity of the order easier to see.
options.misconception: mistakes repetition of a record for evidence about necessity

options.text: Draw the sequence on the sheet, since a diagram demonstrates necessity better than a written claim.
options.misconception: believes a diagram can demonstrate necessity on its own

questions.explanation: Showing that an ordering was necessary needs a case where reversing it would have produced a wrong result, which separates necessity from preference. Efficiency and repetition show nothing of the sort.
questions.hint: Ask what would have gone wrong in the other order.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing structures and comparing sequences
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a structural comparison from a sequential one
questions.stem: A cartographer compares two mapped coastlines: one with a single deep inlet, one with a chain of small bays. What is the difference between comparing their structures and comparing their sequences?

options.text: Structure comparison asks what the features are, while sequence comparison asks when they were mapped.
options.misconception: reduces sequence comparison to a question of survey dates

options.text: Structure comparison looks for a shared arrangement, while sequence comparison looks for the order in which events ran.
options.misconception: mistakes a sequence comparison for a search for a shared layout

options.text: Structure comparison concerns the arrangement of the features, while sequence comparison concerns the order of events that produced them.
Structure comparison is the older practice, while sequence comparison only became possible with digital mapping.
options.misconception: ranks the two practices by the date of their invention

questions.explanation: A structural comparison asks whether parts and their arrangement resemble one another; a sequential one asks about the order of events. The two can disagree about a pair, and neither depends on tools.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison is about shapes or about order.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Combining a count with an account of what happened
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a count and a detailed survey support together
questions.stem: A cartographer has a count of eleven harbours where the coastline is misrepresented and one detailed survey of a misrepresented harbour. Explain what combining the two supports.

answer.exemplar: The count and the detailed survey carry different claims, and putting them together is worthwhile because the count says the misrepresentation is widespread across eleven harbours, while the survey says how the distortion arises in one of them, which the count alone cannot show. The combination therefore supports a statement that this kind of misrepresentation recurs and a separate statement that it comes about in a particular way. What the combination does not support is a single settled explanation for all eleven harbours, since the detailed survey was made in one place and the reasons elsewhere may differ, and it does not turn the eleven into a rate, because the denominator of all harbours surveyed is not in evidence.

questions.explanation: The count shows the misrepresentation recurs across eleven harbours, and the survey shows how it arises in one, so together they support a pattern and a mechanism. One survey cannot explain eleven harbours.
questions.hint: Ask what the count shows that the survey cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Ranking sources depends on the question being asked
questions.learningObjective: Rank sources by the question being asked

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes compare two sources for the position of a river mouth: an eighteenth-century survey carried out from the water, and a recent aerial survey. The notes record that the earlier survey is the only record of the mouth before a harbour wall was built, and that the later survey is more accurate for the present position of the shoreline.

questions.stem: Given this note, which source should be preferred and why?

options.text: The aerial survey, because a later and more accurate source always outweighs an earlier one.
options.misconception: ranks sources by recency and accuracy regardless of the question

options.text: The older survey, because the earlier record is closer to the original conditions being asked about.
options.misconception: ranks sources by closeness to the original whatever the question

options.text: Neither, because a source that is more accurate for one question cannot be used for another question at all.
options.misconception: treats a source as useless for any question it does not fit best

options.text: It depends on the question, since each source is the better one for what it alone records.

questions.explanation: Which source is better depends on the question, because each records something the other does not. Accuracy settles nothing until the question is fixed, and neither source is useless elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask which question is being asked before ranking sources.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: Identify the warrant for generalising an exceptional value
questions.stem: A cartographer finds that one surveyed lake is far deeper than the depth recorded for comparable lakes. What warrants treating that depth as representative of the others?

options.text: That the extra depth comes from a cause shown to affect comparable lakes too, such as a shared rock type.
That the survey of that lake was the most careful of the three, since careful work generalises best.
options.misconception: treats care in the survey as a warrant for extending the result

options.text: That the lake was surveyed in the same season as the others, since seasons shape what a survey records.
options.misconception: assumes a shared season makes one reading stand for the rest

options.text: That the depth was measured in the same units as the other figures, since units make a figure comparable.
options.misconception: treats matching units as a warrant for a generalisation

questions.explanation: A deep figure can stand for the others only if the cause of the extra depth also operates there, which a shared rock type would establish. Common units make the measurement sound, not typical.
questions.hint: Ask whether the cause reaches the other lakes.

questions.learningObjective: Record the assumption that a generalisation depends on
questions.stem: A cartographer generalises one river's behaviour to all rivers on a sheet of varied geology. What should the cartographer record to make the generalisation assessable?

options.misconception: offers a reference in place of the assumption the claim rests on

options.text: The assumption that the surveyed river is typical of the others, since that is what the generalisation leans on.
The number of rivers on the sheet, so the reader can judge how large the general class is.
options.misconception: supplies a class size instead of the assumption behind the claim

options.text: A note that the generalisation may be wrong, since a caveat is the same as giving the assumption.
options.misconception: treats a warning as a substitute for the stated assumption

questions.explanation: A generalisation can be assessed only if the assumption it leans on is written down: that the surveyed river is typical of the others. A survey name and a class size do not supply that.
questions.hint: Ask what the generalisation assumes about the river.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: State what a case chosen for its promise can show
questions.stem: A cartographer chooses a stretch of coast with the sharpest cliff in it to test the accuracy of a plotted outline. What does this case promise to show?

options.text: That every stretch of coast on the sheet is outlined as accurately as the sheet's legend claims.
options.misconception: treats one demanding case as a check on the whole sheet

options.text: That the instrument used for the survey was working within its stated tolerance on the day.
options.misconception: reads a case chosen for its promise as a test of the instrument

options.text: That the outline can be trusted where the landform is most demanding, which is where errors show.
That the steepest stretch is the best representative of the whole coastline for survey purposes.
options.misconception: confuses a case chosen to be hard with one chosen to be typical

questions.explanation: A case chosen for its promise is picked to expose what the map claims, and sharp cliffs expose outline errors most clearly. One hard case does not check the sheet, and hard is not the same as typical.
questions.hint: Ask what the map claims and where that claim is most tested.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a deviant case obliges an explanation to add
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a deviant case requires an account to add
questions.stem: A cartographer's plotted forest boundary runs straight through a stand of trees that the survey records as scattered. Explain what the account must now add.

answer.exemplar: The account must now add whatever makes the scattered stand legible on the sheet, which may be a conventional symbol that shows density as texture rather than as an edge, or a decision to draw the boundary in a different manner in that square. The deviant case obliges the account to explain a feature it would otherwise have treated as a single edge, and the point of keeping it is that the explanation has to work for the ordinary stands as well. A cartographer who simply removed the scatter from the sheet would have avoided the difficulty by making the data fit the drawing rather than by showing what the drawing is doing.

questions.explanation: The account must add whatever makes the scattered stand legible on the sheet, and it must work for the ordinary stands too. Removing the scatter would make the data fit the drawing rather than show what it does.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawing must now explain.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for establishing that an ordering was necessary
questions.learningObjective: Find the observation that shows an ordering was necessary

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that the aerial photographs were flown before the field names were collected, and that the field names were collected before the lettering was set. A separate line notes that the photographs would have shown the fields as bare ground, since the crop was not yet in.

questions.stem: Given this note, which observation would show that the order of the photographs and the field names was necessary?

options.text: The note that the photographs were flown first, since a recorded order already establishes necessity.
options.misconception: treats a recorded order as if it already showed necessity

options.text: The note that the field names were collected before the lettering was set, since that is the same kind of ordering.
options.misconception: offers a second ordering as if it showed the first was needed

options.text: The note that the crop was not yet in the ground, since it shows the photographs were unhelpful.
options.misconception: shows photographs were unhelpful, not that the order mattered

options.text: The note that flying the photographs after the names were collected would have shown named fields with no photographs to check them against.

questions.explanation: Showing that an ordering was necessary means showing that the other order would have produced a worse result, and the note about bare fields does that. Recording an order does not settle necessity.
questions.hint: Ask what the other order would have produced.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing structures and comparing sequences
questions.learningObjective: Say what a structural comparison shows that a sequential one does not
questions.stem: Two rivers on one sheet have comparable widths but very different courses. What does a comparison of their structures show that a comparison of their courses does not?

options.text: That the arrangement of bends differs, since one meanders freely and the other runs in straight reaches between hills.
That the rivers reach the sea at different speeds, since a wider river always flows more quickly.
options.misconception: adds a flow claim to a comparison of form

options.text: That the wider river is the older one, since age determines a river's course.
options.misconception: infers an age from a comparison of courses

options.text: That both rivers were surveyed in the same period, since structure reveals the survey dates.
options.misconception: claims the comparison reveals survey dates

questions.explanation: A structural comparison looks at how the parts are arranged, so it shows the difference between a free meander and straight reaches. Speeds, ages and survey dates are separate matters it does not settle.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison concerns arrangement or movement.

options.misconception: treats a small count as enough to establish a pattern

options.text: Report the count and the detailed record separately, since each supports a claim the other cannot.
Use the detailed record to explain all four omissions, since the series was drawn by one team.
options.misconception: extends one detailed account to every affected sheet in the series

options.text: Drop the detailed record, since a count of affected sheets is the stronger form of evidence.
options.misconception: prefers the count to the record for no stated reason

questions.explanation: The count says how many sheets are affected and the record shows what the omission looks like, so each supports a claim the other cannot. Four cases establish no pattern, and one record explains one.

options.misconception: ranks sources by date regardless of the question being asked

options.text: The reputation of the survey team, because the standing of a source settles its fitness for a question.
options.misconception: ranks sources by reputation rather than by what they record

options.text: What the question asks, since the image and the survey record different things and each fits some questions.
The cost of consulting each source, since the cheaper source is the sounder one for the purpose.
options.misconception: ranks sources by price rather than by fitness for the question

questions.explanation: Ranking sources depends on the question, because the image and the field survey record different things and each suits some questions. Recency and reputation are considerations, not the decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the question needs a source to record.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: Explain what warrants widening a correction beyond one case
questions.stem: A cartographer finds that one named height is wrong by twelve metres on the sheet. Explain what would warrant correcting the whole height series.

answer.exemplar: Correcting the whole series would need a warrant that the error is not confined to that one height, and the only kind that does that is a cause shown to operate across the series, such as a shared benchmark whose true value was misestablished. A single misplotted spot supports a correction at that spot and no more, and a cartographer who spread the correction across the sheet on the strength of one bad figure would be correcting many points without evidence for any of them. The right response is to correct the one height, publish the reason, and treat the series as suspect until the benchmarks are checked.

questions.explanation: Correcting the whole series needs a cause operating across it, such as a misestablished benchmark, and one bad spot supports a correction at that spot alone. Spreading it fixes points without evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true of every point on the sheet.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: State the warrant and the limit of a generalisation

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that on one sheet every field boundary was drawn in black and every track in brown, and the legend says so. The notes for a later sheet record that the same conventions were used but that two fields are shown with a broken line, with no legend entry for it. A third line notes that the two fields are the ones where the paper is torn.

questions.stem: Given this note, what does the generalisation about the conventions rest on and what does it not cover?

options.text: It rests on the later sheet's use of the conventions, and it does not cover the earlier sheet at all.
options.misconception: reads the generalisation as resting on a single sheet

options.text: It rests on the legend, and it does not cover any sheet whose legend is missing.
options.misconception: bases a generalisation on a legend rather than on the practice

options.text: It rests on the two torn fields, and it does not cover sheets with no torn paper.
options.misconception: bases the generalisation on a physical defect rather than on a practice

options.text: It rests on the black and brown conventions holding across the sheets, and it does not cover the broken line, which the notes explain otherwise.

questions.explanation: The generalisation rests on the black and brown conventions holding across the sheets, and the broken line is separate, explained by the torn paper. A legend and a torn corner are not the warrant it needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the generalisation covers and what it excludes.

questions.stem: A cartographer checks a projection at a point where two graticule lines cross near a steep ridge, expecting the projection to fail hardest there. What does this case perform?

options.misconception: treats one checked point as a check on the whole sheet

options.misconception: redirects the check toward the survey rather than the projection

options.misconception: redirects the check toward the drawing rather than the projection

questions.explanation: A case chosen for its promise is picked where the map's claim is most exposed, so checking it there gives the projection a fair chance to fail. One point does not test the sheet.
questions.hint: Ask where the projection is most likely to fail.

Leave the plate as it is, since a deviant case is a matter for the field record and not for the published sheet.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing structures and comparing sequences
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what a structural and a historical comparison establish
questions.stem: A cartographer compares two deltas: one built by a single distributary, one by many. Explain what comparing their structures and comparing their histories each establish.

answer.exemplar: Comparing the structures establishes how the two deltas are built: one has a single channel dividing and dividing again, and the other spreads through a network of smaller channels, so the sheet shows a difference in the arrangement of parts. Comparing the histories establishes the order in which the channels formed, which the present arrangement alone cannot reveal, because a network and a single channel can both be reached by more than one sequence of events. The two comparisons answer different questions, and a cartographer who substitutes one for the other will draw conclusions the evidence does not support, such as claiming that a distributary pattern is the result of a particular sequence of floods.

questions.explanation: Comparing structures establishes how the deltas are built, and comparing histories establishes the order the channels formed in. The arrangement cannot reveal that order, and the two comparisons answer different questions.
questions.hint: Ask which question each comparison answers.

questions.topic: Combining a count with an account of what happened
questions.learningObjective: Say what a count of symbols and one exception support

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that on the sheet, nine hundred and forty small settlements are shown as a single dot each, and one settlement is drawn with a small filled square. options.misconception: invents a threshold rule that the notes never record

options.text: That most settlements on the sheet are very small, because a dot is used for the great majority of them.
options.misconception: reads a symbol choice as a direct measurement of population

options.text: That population size was not considered when the symbols were chosen, since the notes record no rule.
options.misconception: concludes a subject was ignored because no rule was written down

options.text: That one settlement is marked differently from the rest, and the notes do not establish the rule that governs the choice.

questions.explanation: The sheet supports the observation that one settlement is marked differently, and the notes support no rule about why. A count of dots shows how many are so marked, not how big they are.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes actually record about symbol choice.

questions.stem: A cartographer must draw a disputed border and has two sources: a treaty text and a field survey of the terrain. What should determine which to follow?

Which source is newer, since the later record is the one that reflects the current understanding.
options.misconception: ranks sources by date without asking what is needed

options.text: Which source is longer, since a fuller record has more to say and so is more likely to be right.
options.misconception: ranks sources by length in place of by fit

options.text: Which source is signed, since a signed document binds more firmly than a survey of the ground.
options.misconception: ranks sources by formality rather than by what the map needs

questions.explanation: What the map is for should decide, because a treaty settles rights and a survey settles where the ground lies. Recency, length and formality do not say which question is in hand.

It does not establish the accuracy of the contours on the gentle ground, which is most of the sheet, because a case chosen for its promise is chosen to be demanding and a demanding case says little about easy ones. answer.exemplar: What should decide the choice is the question being asked, since the two sources record different things: the aerial image shows the marks that are visible on the ground at the time of the flight, and the parish map shows boundaries as a nineteenth-century surveyor understood and drew them. Where the question is about how the boundaries are marked now, the image is the source that answers it, and where the question is about the arrangement a community once recorded, the parish map is the source that answers it. A general preference for one source over the other is not a method, because each is the better record of its own subject and the cartographer's job is to say which subject the map is about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for establishing that an ordering was necessary
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a recorded order does not establish its necessity
questions.stem: A cartographer records that the coast was surveyed before the seam was decided, and that the seam was decided before the sheet was engraved. Explain why this order alone does not show it was necessary.

answer.exemplar: An order alone does not show necessity, because necessity is a claim about what would have happened in the other order, and the notes contain no case of the reversed order. The cartographer has recorded a sequence and nothing more, and the usual way to establish necessity is to point to a step that would have produced a wrong or impossible result had it come earlier, such as engraving a seam before the coast was known, which would have fixed a boundary that the survey then contradicted. Until such a case exists, the recorded order can be described as the order the work happened in, and it can be called necessary only as a statement about one step's dependence on another.

questions.explanation: An order alone does not show necessity, because necessity concerns what would have happened in the other order. A step that would have gone wrong earlier is what would establish the claim.
questions.hint: Ask what would have gone wrong in the other order.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: Set out the warrant behind a claim about what a pattern records
questions.stem: A cartographer writes that the pattern of field boundaries on the sheet shows how the land was enclosed. Explain what this claim rests on and what would make it secure.

answer.exemplar: The claim rests on the warrant that the boundaries recorded on the sheet were drawn the way they were actually traced on the ground, and that what can be read from a pattern of boundaries is a fair record of how the land was enclosed rather than an artefact of how the surveyor chose to represent it. A claim of this kind is weakened when the record shows boundaries drawn by convention, along roads or rivers for the sake of a tidier sheet, because then the pattern shows the drawing rather than the land. The warrant would be secured by field notes that record where the boundaries were traced as they were found, and by at least one section where the pattern can be checked against something on the ground that was not drawn at all.

questions.explanation: The claim rests on the warrant that the boundaries were drawn as traced, so the pattern records the land not the drawing. Field notes of traced boundaries would secure it, and an undrawn check would test it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the drawing shows the land or the convention.

answer.exemplar: Together they support two claims that neither source supports alone: the count says that dry wells are a widespread pattern across the sheet rather than a handful of local accidents, and the account says how one such well came to fail, in terms of the water table and the construction of its shaft. What the pair does not support is a single explanation for all fifty, because the account was made in one place and the reasons for the others may be different, and it does not supply a rate, because the number of wells that have not dried is not in the notes. The honest account gives the pattern and one mechanism, and says which is which.

options.misconception: ranks sources by recency rather than by what each records

options.text: The tithe map, since it was made for the purpose of recording who held what.
options.misconception: ranks sources by the purpose they were made for

options.text: The ordnance sheet, since it plots the hedge itself and therefore shows where it stood.
It depends on the question, and for where the hedge stood the source that plots the hedge is the one that answers it.
options.misconception: treats owners' agreement as proof of the hedge's position

questions.explanation: For a question about where the hedge stood, the source that plots the hedge answers it, since the other two record a boundary and an agreement. Which source is better depends on the question, not on recency.
questions.hint: Ask which source records the feature in the question.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: State the warrant for extending a drawing convention
questions.stem: A cartographer finds that one boundary on the sheet follows a hedge and the rest follow rivers. What warrants drawing that boundary as a hedge elsewhere too?

options.text: That the hedge is shown on the source plan, so the convention can be carried across wherever such a boundary appears.
That the boundary is the oldest on the sheet, since age is the best guide to what a line is.
options.misconception: uses a feature's age as grounds for how it should be drawn

options.text: That the sheet uses hedges for boundaries everywhere, so the one case is the general rule.
options.misconception: generalises from one case to a convention for the whole sheet

options.text: That the boundary is the shortest, since short boundaries are usually older features.
options.misconception: uses a line's length as grounds for the convention it follows

questions.explanation: The warrant is that the source plan shows the hedge, so the convention travels with evidence of what the line is. The age of a line, a sheet convention and the length of a boundary are not grounds.
questions.hint: Ask what the source plan shows about that boundary.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: Write down the assumption a generalisation depends on
questions.stem: A cartographer generalises one village's street pattern to the county's villages. What should the cartographer write down to make the generalisation assessable?

options.text: The date of the survey, since a recent survey is the only thing that can support a generalisation.
options.misconception: takes a survey date in place of a warrant for the claim

options.text: The assumption that the surveyed village is typical of the others, since that is the warrant the claim rests on.
A list of the county's villages, so that the reader can see how many cases the claim covers.
options.misconception: supplies the size of the class in place of the assumption

options.text: A disclaimer, so that a reader knows the claim might be wrong before reading further.
options.misconception: believes a disclaimer performs the work of a stated assumption

questions.explanation: A generalisation can be assessed only if the assumption it rests on is written down: that the surveyed village is typical. A date, a list and a disclaimer give the reader nothing to weigh.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim assumes about the one village.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: Say what a case chosen for its promise tests
questions.stem: A cartographer tests the sheet's representation of a steep escarpment by checking it against the field record. What does this case perform?

options.text: It tests the accuracy of the whole sheet, since every feature is drawn to the same standard.
options.misconception: treats one case as a check on every feature on the sheet

options.text: It tests the field record, since the check could reveal that the record is at fault.
options.misconception: makes a case chosen to test the drawing a test of the record

options.text: It tests the claim that the escarpment is drawn as the field record has it, which is what the case was chosen for.
It tests the grid on which the sheet is drawn, since the escarpment bears on the grid's fit.
options.misconception: redirects the check toward the grid rather than the feature

questions.explanation: A case chosen for its promise is picked to expose what the sheet gets wrong, and the escarpment is where contouring is expected to fail. Checking it tests the drawing, and says nothing about the rest.
questions.hint: Ask what the case was chosen to expose.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a deviant case obliges an explanation to add
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a deviant case requires the account to include
questions.stem: A cartographer's account of a river does not explain why the sheet shows it as it does. Explain what the account now has to include.

answer.exemplar: The account now has to include whatever would let a reader see why the drawing takes the form it does, and that means saying what the river was taken to be: whether the sheet is showing the channel, the flood plain, the line of the valley or a conventional line drawn to fit the page. A deviant case obliges the account to add the element the ordinary case did not require, and here the ordinary case was a river whose drawing needed no explanation because it ran the way rivers do. The obligation is not to change the drawing but to say what the drawing represents, so that a reader is not left guessing, and the account must also make clear whether the unusual form is a feature of the river or a choice made to fit the sheet.

questions.explanation: The account has to include whatever lets a reader see why the drawing takes that form, which means saying what the river was taken to be: channel, flood plain or valley. The obligation is to explain the drawing, not change it.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawing is taken to represent.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for establishing that an ordering was necessary
questions.learningObjective: Assess a recorded order whose links cannot be checked

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that a triangulation of four points was observed, that the heights were computed from those observations, and that the contouring was drawn from the computed heights. A separate line notes that the notes of the observation survive but the intermediate computation sheets do not.

questions.stem: Given this note, what can be said about the order of the stages and its necessity?

options.text: The order is necessary, since computing heights requires observations and contours require computed heights.
options.misconception: takes evident dependence as proof the whole order was necessary

options.text: The order is convenient, since a survey of this kind is usually done in that sequence.
options.misconception: explains an order by the usual way such work is done

options.text: The order is recorded but not shown necessary, and the missing computation sheets mean the middle link cannot be checked at all.
options.misconception: claims the missing sheets make the order untestable

options.text: The order is recorded, and the missing sheets make it harder to test whether reversing it would have mattered.

questions.explanation: The notes record the order of the three stages, and necessity needs a case of the reversed order. The missing sheets do not settle the question, though they make it harder to test.
questions.hint: Ask what the missing sheets would have shown.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Comparing structures and comparing sequences
questions.learningObjective: State what a comparison of form settles and leaves open
questions.stem: A cartographer compares two settlements with the same number of houses, one arranged around a green and one along a road. What does the comparison show, and what does it leave open?

options.text: It shows a difference in arrangement, and it leaves open the order in which either settlement grew.
It shows a difference in size, since the two settlements cannot hold the same number of houses.
options.misconception: contradicts the premise the comparison was set up on

options.text: It shows a difference in history, since the two forms came about in different ways.
options.misconception: reads a difference in arrangement as a difference in history

options.text: It shows that the road settlement is the older one, since linear settlements are usually the earliest.
options.misconception: ranks two settlement forms by age without evidence

questions.explanation: The comparison shows a difference in arrangement, one grouped around a green and one strung along a road, and leaves open the order in which either grew. Form does not settle history.
questions.hint: Ask what the comparison fixes and what it cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Combining a count with an account of what happened
questions.learningObjective: Use a count and a case together without letting one explain the other
questions.stem: A cartographer has a list of thirty unmapped streams and one field survey of a stream that was left off the sheet. What should the cartographer do with the two together?

options.text: Publish the list as the map's deficiency, since thirty omissions are a serious enough record on their own.
options.misconception: treats a count of omissions as a complete account on its own

options.text: Report the count and the surveyed case separately, since each supports a claim the other cannot.
Use the surveyed stream to explain all thirty omissions, since they were all left off by the same editor.
options.misconception: extends one surveyed case to every case in the list

options.text: Use the list to explain the surveyed stream, since a list of similar cases explains any one case.
options.misconception: reverses the relationship and lets a list explain a detailed case

questions.explanation: The count says how many streams were left off and the survey shows what such an omission looks like, so each supports a claim the other cannot. One case cannot explain thirty, nor a list one case.
questions.hint: Ask what each source can show that the other cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Ranking sources depends on the question being asked
questions.learningObjective: Decide between sources by coverage and scale
questions.stem: A cartographer must choose between a large-scale survey of one district and a small-scale survey of a whole region, for a question about a proposed route. What should decide the choice?

options.text: The scale of each source, since the larger scale is always the better source for any question.
options.misconception: prefers large scale as a general rule regardless of the question

options.text: The size of the area covered, since a smaller area always contains more usable detail.
options.misconception: prefers small coverage as a general rule regardless of the question

options.text: Which of the two covers the ground the question is about at a scale that shows what matters.
The date of each survey, since an older sheet records more of what was there before the changes.
options.misconception: prefers an older record because it shows the past

questions.explanation: The choice turns on whether a source covers the ground the question is about at a scale that shows what matters. A large-scale sheet of the wrong district is no use, and scale matters only in relation to the question.
questions.hint: Ask which ground and which scale the question needs.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What warrants carrying a claim past one case
questions.learningObjective: Make a generalisation from one case legitimate
questions.stem: A cartographer has one case in which the ground rises in a way the sheet does not show, and wishes to generalise from it. Explain what the cartographer must do to make the generalisation legitimate.

answer.exemplar: To make the generalisation legitimate, the cartographer has to establish that the case is not an accident of the ground but a case of something that also operates elsewhere on the sheet, and to say what that something is. If the rise is shown on the same sheet to occur wherever a particular rock meets a particular slope, then the case is representative of a rule and the rule can be generalised; if the rise is confined to one spot, the case is exceptional and nothing can be carried past it. The work therefore consists in finding the features the case shares with the rest of the sheet, and in writing down the generalisation as a claim about those features rather than about the case itself.

questions.explanation: To generalise legitimately, the cartographer must show the case is not an accident but an instance of something operating elsewhere, and say what that is. If the rise is in one spot, nothing carries past it.
questions.hint: Ask what the case shares with the rest of the sheet.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The warrant behind a case-based generalisation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the unmet condition in a generalisation about records

stimulus.body: A cartographer's notes record that the tide marks shown on the sheet were copied from a set of levelling records made in a single year. The notes for a later sheet record that the tide marks were taken from records gathered in three separate years. The notes add that the two sheets cover coastlines with very different tidal ranges.

questions.stem: Given these notes, what does the generalisation about tide marks rest on?

options.text: It rests on the practice of copying tide marks from levelling records, since both sheets do that.
options.misconception: takes a shared procedure as a sufficient warrant

options.text: It rests on the later sheet's three years of records, since more records make a safer generalisation.
options.misconception: believes more records make a generalisation automatically safer

options.text: It rests on the two sheets sharing a coastline, since only then can the practice be compared at all.
options.misconception: requires a shared coastline before any comparison is possible

options.text: It rests on the single-year records applying beyond their year and beyond their tidal range, which the notes do not show.

questions.explanation: The generalisation rests on the single-year records applying beyond their year and tidal range, and the notes show neither. A shared procedure and more records are not warrants for that step.
questions.hint: Ask whether the later sheet's coastlines match in tidal range.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The test a case chosen for its promise performs
questions.learningObjective: State what a promising case tests and leaves open
questions.stem: A cartographer chooses a town where the road and the river cross at a bridge, to check how the sheet shows crossings. What does this case test and what does it leave open?

options.text: It tests how crossings are shown where two features coincide, and it leaves open how such crossings are shown elsewhere.
It tests the whole system of showing crossings, since one case is a fair sample of them all.
options.misconception: treats one case as a fair sample of the whole practice

options.text: It tests the accuracy of the river, since a bridge on the map is a mark of where the river was surveyed.
options.misconception: redirects the check to the survey of the river

options.text: It tests the road classification, since a bridge on the map shows the class of the road that crosses.
options.misconception: reads a drawn feature as evidence of a classification

questions.explanation: The case tests how the sheet shows crossings where two features coincide, and one such place says nothing about crossings elsewhere. The survey of the river and the road's class are separate matters.
questions.hint: Ask what the case was chosen to expose and what follows.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a deviant case obliges an explanation to add
questions.learningObjective: Act on a deviant case without discarding the drawing
questions.stem: A cartographer's sheet shows a lake with a smooth outline, and the field record describes a marshy, indented shore. What should the cartographer do?

options.text: Redraw the lake with the indented shore, since the field record is the more detailed evidence of the ground.
options.misconception: assumes the more detailed record must decide the published form

options.text: Keep the sheet and add an account of what the smooth outline is standing for, so both records can be read.
Leave the sheet alone, since a smooth lake outline is a long-standing convention on maps of the area.
options.misconception: treats a convention as beyond challenge from the field record

options.text: Add a note that the two accounts differ, since the difference itself is the honest result.
options.misconception: believes reporting a difference is the same as accounting for it

questions.explanation: A deviant case obliges the account to say what the smooth outline stands for, so the drawing and the record can be read together. Redrawing discards the sheet, and noting the difference accounts for nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the outline is standing for on the sheet.
